A lot of people do have some sort of coverage through work, and there's nothing wrong with that at all. In many cases, the employer gives a small amount of protection at little to no cost, so it can absolutely be a good starting point for families. The biggest thing people don't always realize, though, is that work coverage is usually tied directly to the job itself. So if somebody retires, changes companies, gets laid off, or becomes too sick to continue working, there's a chance that coverage could reduce or disappear right when the family may need protection the most. Another thing families sometimes run into is lack of control. Since the employer controls the policy, the benefits and long-term availability can change over time based on the company's decisions rather than yours. That's why many families choose to have something personal in place that they fully own and control themselves — so no matter what happens with work, health, or retirement later on, they know their loved ones still have protection they can count on.

At the end of the day, the biggest difference really comes down to temporary protection versus permanent protection. Term insurance can make a lot of sense for families trying to protect temporary responsibilities during the heavier financial years of life — things like a mortgage, raising children, replacing income, or covering debt while keeping the monthly payment lower. Whole life insurance is usually more about long-term certainty and making sure there is protection in place no matter when that day eventually comes. A lot of families like knowing the coverage is designed to stay with them for life instead of potentially expiring later on when age or health may make it difficult to qualify again. The reality is that life changes, health changes, and eventually we all pass away at some point. That's why many families feel more comfortable having at least some permanent protection in place, so the people they love are not left trying to figure everything out alone later on. At the end of the day, this is not really about choosing the "most expensive" policy or the "cheapest" policy. It's about making sure your family has protection they can truly depend on when they need it most.

Term life insurance is designed more for temporary responsibilities during the heavier financial years of life. So for example, while the mortgage is high, the kids are still young, or the family is depending heavily on your income, term coverage can help create a financial safety net during those years. A lot of families like term because it usually allows them to get a larger amount of protection for a lower monthly payment upfront. The tradeoff is that term coverage is designed to eventually expire after a certain number of years. So the question families usually ask themselves is: "Will I still want protection later in life after the term ends?" Because if coverage expires later on and health changes with age, it can become harder or much more expensive to replace that protection down the road.

Whole life insurance is designed for families who want protection that stays in place for life instead of expiring after a temporary period of time. A lot of people like the peace of mind that comes from knowing that no matter what happens with age or health later on, they've already got something in place their family can depend on. Unlike temporary coverage, whole life is built to stay with you permanently as long as premiums are paid. The premiums are typically fixed, meaning they don't continue increasing because of age or declining health later in life. Many whole life policies can build cash value over time and may include living benefits as well, which can help if life ever takes an unexpected turn through things like serious illness, disability, or major health events. At the end of the day, the biggest difference really comes down to temporary protection versus permanent protection. Temporary coverage can absolutely make sense for temporary needs. But many families feel more comfortable knowing they have at least some permanent protection in place because the reality is, the need for life insurance itself does not disappear.
